claim: Ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) fulfill an important role in communication and navigation in many species.
source: Ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) fulfill an important role in communication and navigation in many species.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: Rodent USVs are increasingly used as a behavioral measure in neurodevelopmental and neurolinguistic research.
source: Because of their social and affective significance, rodent USVs are increasingly used as a behavioral measure in neurodevelopmental and neurolinguistic research.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context of the research field and citations provided in the introduction.

claim: Reliably attributing USVs to their emitter during close interactions has emerged as a difficult, key challenge.
source: Reliably attributing USVs to their emitter during close interactions has emerged as a difficult, key challenge.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field based on the context of existing research.

claim: HyVL is the first to achieve millimeter precision (~3.4–4.8 mm, 91% assigned) in localizing USVs.
source: HyVL is the first to achieve millimeter precision (~3.4–4.8 mm, 91% assigned) in localizing USVs, ~3× better than other systems, approaching the physical limits (mouse snout ~10 mm).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3.

claim: HyVL achieves ~3× better localization precision than other systems.
source: HyVL is the first to achieve millimeter precision (~3.4–4.8 mm, 91% assigned) in localizing USVs, ~3× better than other systems, approaching the physical limits (mouse snout ~10 mm).
evidence: This is a comparative claim supported by data comparing HyVL to previous methods like SLIM.

claim: HyVL approaches the physical limits of localization (mouse snout ~10 mm).
source: HyVL is the first to achieve millimeter precision (~3.4–4.8 mm, 91% assigned) in localizing USVs, ~3× better than other systems, approaching the physical limits (mouse snout ~10 mm).
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical dimensions of the mouse snout and the achieved accuracy.

claim: Males and females vocalize in starkly different relative spatial positions during courtship interactions.
source: We analyze mouse courtship interactions and demonstrate that males and females vocalize in starkly different relative spatial positions, and that the fraction of female vocalizations has likely been overestimated previously due to imprecise localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The fraction of female vocalizations has likely been overestimated previously due to imprecise localization.
source: We analyze mouse courtship interactions and demonstrate that males and females vocalize in starkly different relative spatial positions, and that the fraction of female vocalizations has likely been overestimated previously due to imprecise localization.
evidence: This is supported by comparing HyVL results with previous methods (SLIM) showing lower female vocalization fractions with higher precision.

claim: When two male mice interact with one female, one of the males takes a dominant role in the interaction both in terms of the vocalization rate and the location relative to the female.
source: Further, we find that when two male mice interact with one female, one of the males takes a dominant role in the interaction both in terms of the vocalization rate and the location relative to the female.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 6 showing vocalization rates and spatial positioning.

claim: USVs have been shown to be present innately and to have significance at multiple stages of life, from neonates to adults.
source: In many of these species, USVs have been shown to be present innately and to have significance at multiple stages of life, from neonates (Kikusui et al., 2011) to adults (Mahrt et al., 2013), often with diverse functions as distress/alarm calls (Kikusui et al., 2011; Litvin et al., 2007), courtship signals (Marconi et al., 2020), territorial defense signals (Rieger and Marler, 2018), private communication (Ramsier et al., 2012), and echolocation (Schnitzler et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: USVs have diverse functions including distress/alarm calls, courtship signals, territorial defense signals, private communication, and echolocation.
source: In many of these species, USVs have been shown to be present innately and to have significance at multiple stages of life, from neonates (Kikusui et al., 2011) to adults (Mahrt et al., 2013), often with diverse functions as distress/alarm calls (Kikusui et al., 2011; Litvin et al., 2007), courtship signals (Marconi et al., 2020), territorial defense signals (Rieger and Marler, 2018), private communication (Ramsier et al., 2012), and echolocation (Schnitzler et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: USVs have been extensively studied in mice, where their communicative significance has been widely demonstrated by their influence on conspecific behavior.
source: USVs have been extensively studied in mice, where their communicative significance has been widely demonstrated by their influence on conspecific behavior (Hammerschmidt et al., 2009; Pultorak et al., 2017; Chabout et al., 2015; Musolf et al., 2015; Sugimoto et al., 2011; Tschida et al., 2019; also in line with observational studies; Warren et al., 2020; Nicolakis et al., 2020; Rieger et al., 2021; Petric and Kalcounis-Rueppell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: USVs can be grouped into different types that are highly context-dependent.
source: USVs can be grouped into different types that are highly context-dependent (Chabout et al., 2015; Musolf et al., 2015; Nicolakis et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021; de Chaumont et al., 2021; Castellucci et al., 2018; Pultorak et al., 2018; Burke et al., 2018; Zala et al., 2017a; Mun et al., 2015; von Merten et al., 2014; Scattoni et al., 2009; Warren et al., 2021; Dou et al., 2018; Hoier et al., 2016; Chabout et al., 2012), and USV syntax itself is predictive of USV sequence (Hertz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: USV syntax itself is predictive of USV sequence.
source: USVs can be grouped into different types that are highly context-dependent (Chabout et al., 2015; Musolf et al., 2015; Nicolakis et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021; de Chaumont et al., 2021; Castellucci et al., 2018; Pultorak et al., 2018; Burke et al., 2018; Zala et al., 2017a; Mun et al., 2015; von Merten et al., 2014; Scattoni et al., 2009; Warren et al., 2021; Dou et al., 2018; Hoier et al., 2016; Chabout et al., 2012), and USV syntax itself is predictive of USV sequence (Hertz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hertz et al., 2020.

claim: The current literature suggests USVs convey affective and social information in different behavioral contexts.
source: Taken together, the current literature suggests USVs convey affective and social information in different behavioral contexts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the body of literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: Testosterone and oxytocin have a modulatory effect on USV production.
source: This is further supported by the modulatory effect that testosterone and oxytocin have on USV production (Kikusui et al., 2021b; Kikusui et al., 2021a; Timonin et al., 2018; Pultorak et al., 2015; Guoynes and Marler, 2021; Tsuji et al., 2021; Tsuji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The neuronal circuitry underlying USVs has recently been identified and is being studied extensively.
source: Importantly, the neuronal circuitry underlying USVs has recently been identified and is being studied extensively (Tschida et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021; Michael et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2019; Tasaka et al., 2018; Fröhlich et al., 2017; Shepard et al., 2016; Arriaga and Jarvis, 2013; Fujita et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Mouse USVs are increasingly being used as a behavioral measure in neurodevelopmental and neurolinguistic translational research.
source: Because of their social and affective significance and our growing mechanistic understanding, mouse USVs are increasingly being used as a behavioral measure in neurodevelopmental and neurolinguistic translational research (de Chaumont et al., 2021; von Merten et al., 2014; Fröhlich et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021; Binder et al., 2021; Hepbasli et al., 2021; Agarwalla et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2012; Hodges et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Ultrasonic vocalizations serve as a biomarker for animal well-being and normal development in various disease models.
source: Their manipulation and precise measurement not only provide the basis for tackling many fundamental questions but also pave the way, via advanced animal models, for the discovery of essential, novel drug targets for many debilitating conditions such as autism-spectrum disorder (Tsai et al., 2012; Silverman et al., 2010), Parkinson's disease (Ciucci et al., 2009), stroke-induced aphasia (Palmateer et al., 2016), epilepsy aphasia syndromes (Erata et al., 2021), progressive language disorders (Menuet et al., 2011), chronic pain (Palazzo et al., 2008), and depression/anxiety disorders (Moskal and Burgdorf, 2018), where ultrasonic vocalizations serve as a biomarker for animal well-being and normal development.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on disease models.

claim: Substantial advances have been made in recent years in USV detection, classification, and localization.
source: In recent years, substantial advances have been made in USV detection (Coffey et al., 2019; Fonseca et al., 2021; Zala et al., 2017b; Van Segbroeck et al., 2017; Chabout et al., 2017), classification (Coffey et al., 2019; Fonseca et al., 2021; Van Segbroeck et al., 2017; Ivanenko et al., 2020), and localization (Oliveira-Stahl et al., 2023; Heckman et al., 2017; Warren et al., 2018a; Neunuebel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Localization is of particular importance during social interactions, when most USVs are emitted.
source: Localization is of particular importance during social interactions, when most USVs are emitted and any meaningful analysis of USV properties rests on a reliable assignment of each USV to its emitter.
evidence: This is supported by the context of the research and data showing most USVs occur during close interactions (Figure 1D).

claim: Most USVs are emitted at close range during social interactions.
source: This task is complex for multiple reasons: (i) most USVs are emitted at close range, (ii) social behavior often requires free movement of the animals, and (iii) USV production is invisible (Chabout et al., 2012; Mahrt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data in Figure 1D showing distance distributions.

claim: USV production is invisible.
source: This task is complex for multiple reasons: (i) most USVs are emitted at close range, (ii) social behavior often requires free movement of the animals, and (iii) USV production is invisible (Chabout et al., 2012; Mahrt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent advances in acoustic localization have improved the localization accuracy to 11–14 mm.
source: Recent advances in acoustic localization (Heckman et al., 2017; Warren et al., 2018a; Neunuebel et al., 2015) have improved the localization accuracy to 11–14 mm; however, close-up snout–snout interactions – which is when a large fraction of USVs are emitted – require an even higher precision.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research methods.

claim: Close-up snout–snout interactions require higher precision than 11–14 mm for reliable USV assignment.
source: Recent advances in acoustic localization (Heckman et al., 2017; Warren et al., 2018a; Neunuebel et al., 2015) have improved the localization accuracy to 11–14 mm; however, close-up snout–snout interactions – which is when a large fraction of USVs are emitted – require an even higher precision.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical dimensions of mice and the frequency of close interactions.

claim: HyVL integrates a high-resolution 'acoustic camera' consisting of 64 ultrasound microphones with an array of four high-quality ultrasound microphones.
source: We have developed an advanced localization system for USVs in which is a high-resolution 'acoustic camera' consisting of 64 ultrasound microphones with an array of four high-quality ultrasound microphones.
evidence: This is a description of the system design presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both the Cam64 and USM4 systems can individually localize USVs but exhibit rather complementary patterns of localization errors.
source: Both systems can individually localize USVs but exhibit rather complementary patterns of localization errors.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A showing the L-shaped error pattern.

claim: HyVL achieves a median absolute localization error of 3.4–4.8 mm.
source: We achieve a median absolute localization error of 3.4–4.8 mm, translating to an assignment rate of ~91%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: HyVL achieves an assignment rate of ~91%.
source: We achieve a median absolute localization error of 3.4–4.8 mm, translating to an assignment rate of ~91%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: HyVL represents a threefold improvement in accuracy compared to the previous state of the art.
source: Compared to the previous state of the art (Oliveira-Stahl et al., 2023; Warren et al., 2018a), the accuracy represents a threefold improvement that halves the proportion of previously unassigned USVs.
evidence: This is supported by comparing HyVL performance to SLIM and other methods.

claim: HyVL halves the proportion of previously unassigned USVs compared to previous methods.
source: Compared to the previous state of the art (Oliveira-Stahl et al., 2023; Warren et al., 2018a), the accuracy represents a threefold improvement that halves the proportion of previously unassigned USVs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the improvement in assignment rate from ~80% to ~91%.

claim: HyVL's accuracy likely approaches the physical limit of localizability for USVs given the physical dimensions of the mouse snout (ø ~10 mm).
source: Given the physical dimensions of the mouse snout (ø ~10 mm), this likely approaches the physical limit of localizability for USVs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the achieved accuracy to the physical size of the sound source.

claim: In triadic recordings, one male takes a dominant role in competitive male–male–female courtship, emitting most USVs and positioning itself more closely to the female abdomen.
source: Further, in the triadic recordings we find that in competitive male–male–female courtship, one male takes a dominant role, which shows in emitting most USVs and also positioning itself more closely to the female abdomen.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Most USVs in the present paradigm were emitted in close proximity to the interaction partners, with the vast majority within 10 cm snout–snout distance.
source: (D) Most USVs in the present paradigm were emitted in close proximity to the interaction partners, with the vast majority within 10 cm snout–snout distance (i.e., ~93 and 72% for dyadic and triadic, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ~93% of USVs in dyadic interactions were emitted within 10 cm snout–snout distance.
source: (D) Most USVs in the present paradigm were emitted in close proximity to the interaction partners, with the vast majority within 10 cm snout–snout distance (i.e., ~93 and 72% for dyadic and triadic, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ~72% of USVs in triadic interactions were emitted within 10 cm snout–snout distance.
source: (D) Most USVs in the present paradigm were emitted in close proximity to the interaction partners, with the vast majority within 10 cm snout–snout distance (i.e., ~93 and 72% for dyadic and triadic, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Cam64 microphones are of lower quality than the USM4 microphones, evidenced by the rising noise floor for higher frequencies.
source: (C) Sample spectrograms from the four ultrasonic microphones and the average of all Cam64 microphones for a bout of vocalizations (start/end times marked by green/red dots). The Cam64 microphones are of lower quality than the USM4 microphones, evidenced by the rising noise floor for higher frequencies, affecting very-high-frequency USVs.
evidence: This is supported by visual comparison in Figure 1C and spectral analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rising noise floor of Cam64 microphones affects very-high-frequency USVs.
source: (C) Sample spectrograms from the four ultrasonic microphones and the average of all Cam64 microphones for a bout of vocalizations (start/end times marked by green/red dots). The Cam64 microphones are of lower quality than the USM4 microphones, evidenced by the rising noise floor for higher frequencies, affecting very-high-frequency USVs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The high-quality ultrasonic microphones had a rather flat baseline noise level across frequency, with the only exception of an ~10 dB deviation for low frequencies.
source: (A) The high-quality ultrasonic microphones (gray: 4× individual, black: average) had a rather flat baseline noise level across frequency, with the only exception of an ~10 dB deviation for low frequencies, far below the relevant frequency range contained in USVs (red overlay).
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Cam64 MEMS microphones have a highly frequency-dependent baseline noise across frequency.
source: (B) The Cam64 micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) microphones (gray: 64× individual, black: average, Akustica AKU242) have a highly frequency-dependent baseline noise across frequency.
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The substantial rise of the noise level for higher frequencies in Cam64 microphones poses an issue for detecting very high frequencies.
source: The peaks at frequencies <50 kHz are less relevant for USV detection, while the substantial rise of the noise level for higher frequencies poses an issue for detecting very high frequencies as their contribution to the recorded signal gets progressively buried in the baseline noise (see Figure 1C for the effect on the detectability of high-frequency USVs).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Figure 1C.

claim: The Cam64 data is processed using acoustic beamforming, which delivers highly precise estimates (median absolute errors [MAE] = ~4–5 mm).
source: The Cam64 data is processed using acoustic beamforming (Van Veen and Buckley, 1988), which delivers highly precise estimates (median absolute errors [MAE] = ~4–5 mm), but is not sensitive enough for very-high-frequency USVs (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Cam64 beamforming is not sensitive enough for very-high-frequency USVs.
source: The Cam64 data is processed using acoustic beamforming (Van Veen and Buckley, 1988), which delivers highly precise estimates (median absolute errors [MAE] = ~4–5 mm), but is not sensitive enough for very-high-frequency USVs (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The USM4 data is analyzed using the previously published SLIM algorithm, which delivers accurate (MAE = ~11–14 mm) and less frequency-limited estimates.
source: The USM4 data is analyzed using the previously published SLIM algorithm (Oliveira-Stahl et al., 2023), which delivers accurate (MAE = ~11–14 mm) and less frequency-limited estimates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data in Figure 3.

claim: SLIM is the previously most accurate ultrasonic localization technique.
source: The accuracy of SLIM, the previously most accurate ultrasonic localization technique (see 'Discussion' for a comparison), is generally lower than that of HyVL, but it makes essential contributions to the overall accuracy of HyVL through the integration of the complementary strength of the two methods/microphone arrays (see Figure 3A and L, shape of errors).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by comparison with other methods in the Discussion.

claim: The methods (Cam64 and USM4/SLIM) exhibit a complementary pattern of localization errors, which predestines them for high synergy when combined.
source: The methods exhibit a complementary pattern of localization errors, which predestines them for high synergy when combined (see below).
evidence: This is supported by the L-shaped error pattern shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For each USV, the Cam64 localization was chosen if its SNR >5, otherwise the USM4/SLIM estimate was used.
source: For each USV, the Cam64 localization was chosen if its SNR >5, otherwise the USM4/SLIM estimate was used (for details, see 'Localization of ultrasonic vocalizations').
evidence: This is a description of the method used in the analysis.

claim: The vast majority of USVs is localized with very small errors for both methods, concentrated close to the axes.
source: (A) The vast majority of USVs is localized with very small errors for both methods, concentrated close to the axes and thus hardly visible, evidenced by the median absolute errors (MAE) for Cam64 (light red line) and SLIM (light green line).
evidence: This is supported by data visualization in Figure 3A.

claim: The fewer larger errors form an L-shape, emphasizing the synergy of a hybrid approach that compensates for the weaknesses of each method.
source: The fewer larger errors form an L-shape, emphasizing the synergy of a hybrid approach that compensates for the weaknesses of each method.
evidence: This is supported by data visualization in Figure 3A.

claim: HyVL enables the localization of 91.1% of all USVs, achieving an MAE = 4.8 mm.
source: (B) The hybrid localization system Hybrid Vocalization Localizer (HyVL) (orange) combines the virtues of SLIM and Cam64 enabling the localization of 91.1% of all USVs (light orange), achieving an MAE = 4.8 mm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: SLIM-based localization only includes 79.8% of all USVs, at an MAE = 14.8 mm.
source: SLIM-based localization (green) only includes 79.8% of all USVs, at an MAE = 14.8 mm (light green, see 'USV assignment' for details on the relation between accuracy and selection criteria).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: For the far condition (animals >100 mm apart), virtually all USVs (332/339, 97.9%) were assigned at an MAE = 3.79 mm.
source: (C) USVs emitted when all animals were >100 mm apart and a single mouse condition was used to assess the ideal accuracy of HyVL. For the far condition, virtually all USVs (332/339, 97.9%) were assigned at an MAE = 3.79 mm, similarly to the single animal condition (MAE = 3.45 mm, 251/255, 98.4%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C.

claim: For the single animal condition, the MAE = 3.45 mm with 251/255 (98.4%) USVs assigned.
source: (C) USVs emitted when all animals were >100 mm apart and a single mouse condition was used to assess the ideal accuracy of HyVL. For the far condition, virtually all USVs (332/339, 97.9%) were assigned at an MAE = 3.79 mm, similarly to the single animal condition (MAE = 3.45 mm, 251/255, 98.4%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C.

claim: The position of the closest animal aligned precisely with the estimated position in both dimensions, indicated by the high density along the diagonal (Pearson r > 0.99 for both dimensions).
source: Next, we inspected separate localization along the X and Y axis to check for anisotropies of localization (Figure 3D/E, histograms normalized to maximum). The position of the closest animal aligned precisely with the estimated position in both dimensions, indicated by the high density along the diagonal (Pearson r > 0.99 for both dimensions) and the MAE's along the X and Y direction separately (X = 3.1 mm, Y = 2.8 mm).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The MAE along the X direction is 3.1 mm and along the Y direction is 2.8 mm.
source: The position of the closest animal aligned precisely with the estimated position in both dimensions, indicated by the high density along the diagonal (Pearson r > 0.99 for both dimensions) and the MAE's along the X and Y direction separately (X = 3.1 mm, Y = 2.8 mm).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: HyVL provides a substantial improvement in the localization precision compared to other methods.
source: In summary, the HyVL system provides a substantial improvement in the localization precision. In comparison to other methods, its precision also allows a larger fraction of vocalizations to be reliably assigned and retained for later analysis, which enables a near complete analysis of vocal communication between mice or other vocal animals (see 'Discussion' for details).
evidence: This is supported by comparative data throughout Figure 3.

claim: HyVL's precision allows a larger fraction of vocalizations to be reliably assigned and retained for later analysis.
source: In summary, the HyVL system provides a substantial improvement in the localization precision. In comparison to other methods, its precision also allows a larger fraction of vocalizations to be reliably assigned and retained for later analysis, which enables a near complete analysis of vocal communication between mice or other vocal animals (see 'Discussion' for details).
evidence: This is supported by the assignment rate data in Figure 3.

claim: Previous studies using a single microphone have often assumed that only the male mouse vocalized.
source: Previous studies using a single microphone have often assumed that only the male mouse vocalized (Rotschafer et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2011; Pomerantz and Clemens, 1981; Nunez et al., 1978), while more recent research has concluded that female mice vocalize as well (Neunuebel et al., 2015; Sangiamo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: More recent research has concluded that female mice vocalize as well.
source: Previous studies using a single microphone have often assumed that only the male mouse vocalized (Rotschafer et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2011; Pomerantz and Clemens, 1981; Nunez et al., 1978), while more recent research has concluded that female mice vocalize as well (Neunuebel et al., 2015; Sangiamo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Female vocalizations were typically less frequent, but constituted a substantial fraction of the vocalizations (11–18%).
source: Female vocalizations were typically less frequent, but constituted a substantial fraction of the vocalizations (11–18%) (Oliveira-Stahl et al., 2023; Heckman et al., 2017; Neunuebel et al., 2015; Warren et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Over all dyadic and triadic trials combined, females produced the minority of vocalizations.
source: Over all dyadic and triadic trials combined, females produced the minority of vocalizations. Naive estimation without MPI selection using SLIM estimates ~14%, while HyVL tallies it at just 7% (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: Naive estimation without MPI selection using SLIM estimates ~14% female vocalizations, while HyVL tallies it at just 7%.
source: Over all dyadic and triadic trials combined, females produced the minority of vocalizations. Naive estimation without MPI selection using SLIM estimates ~14%, while HyVL tallies it at just 7% (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: Applying MPI selection, SLIM estimates only 5.5% female vocalizations, while HyVL arrives at significantly less, just 4.4% (p=0.002).
source: Applying MPI selection, SLIM estimates only 5.5%, while HyVL arrives at significantly less, just 4.4% (p=0.002, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 4A/B), while reliably classifying 91.1% of all vocalizations.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4A/B.

claim: Using the hybrid method instead of SLIM significantly reduces the fraction of female vocalizations.
source: (B) Using the hybrid method instead of SLIM significantly reduces the fraction of female vocalizations, suggesting that less accurate algorithms overestimate the female fraction (only results for MPI-selected USVs shown).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Less accurate algorithms overestimate the female fraction of vocalizations.
source: (B) Using the hybrid method instead of SLIM significantly reduces the fraction of female vocalizations, suggesting that less accurate algorithms overestimate the female fraction (only results for MPI-selected USVs shown).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between SLIM and HyVL results.

claim: Considering only vocalizations that are emitted when the snouts are >50 mm apart further significantly reduces the fraction to female USVs to 1.1% after MPI selection (p=5.2 × 10–8).
source: Considering only vocalizations that are emitted when the snouts are >50 mm apart further significantly reduces the fraction to female USVs to 1.1% after MPI selection (p=5.2 × 10–8, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Female mice vocalize preferentially in close snout–snout contact.
source: (C) The fraction of female vocalizations further reduces if only USVs are considered that are emitted while all animal snouts were >50 mm apart from each other. This indicates a preference of female mice to vocalize in close snout–snout contact; however, this entails that female vocalizations are more prone to confusion with male vocalizations due to their relative spatial occurrence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduction in female vocalization fraction when close interactions are excluded.

claim: Female vocalizations are more prone to confusion with male vocalizations due to their relative spatial occurrence.
source: (C) The fraction of female vocalizations further reduces if only USVs are considered that are emitted while all animal snouts were >50 mm apart from each other. This indicates a preference of female mice to vocalize in close snout–snout contact; however, this entails that female vocalizations are more prone to confusion with male vocalizations due to their relative spatial occurrence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of vocalizations.

claim: There was no difference in the female fraction of USVs between dyadic and triadic pairings.
source: Comparing the percentage of female vocalizations between dyadic and triadic trials, no significant differences were found (p=0.22, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4D.

claim: Female mice appear to emit vocalizations in very close snout–snout contact, with a small fraction of vocalizations also occurring when the male mouse around the hind-paws/ano-genital region.
source: (F) Female mice appear to emit vocalizations in very close snout–snout contact, with a small fraction of vocalizations also occurring when the male mouse around the hind-paws/ano-genital region.
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis data in Figure 4F.

claim: Male mice emit vocalizations both in snout–snout contact, but also at greater distances, which dominantly correspond to a close approach of the male's snout to the female ano-genital region.
source: (G) Male mice emit vocalizations both in snout–snout contact, but also at greater distances, which dominantly correspond to a close approach of the male's snout to the female ano-genital region. This was verified separately with a corresponding analysis, where the recipient's tail-onset was used instead (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis data in Figure 4G.

claim: Radial distance density of receiver animals shows a significant difference, with females vocalizing mostly when males are in close proximity of the snout, while males vocalize when the female mouse's snout is very close or about 1 body length away.
source: (H) Radial distance density of receiver animals, marginalized over directions, shows a significant difference, with females vocalizing mostly when males (blue) are in close proximity of the snout, while males vocalize when the female mouse's snout is very close (corresponding to snout-snout contact), but also when the female's snout is about 1 body length away (snout–ano-genital interaction). Plots show means and SEM confidence bounds.
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis data in Figure 4H.

claim: Female mice vocalize primarily when the male mouse's snout is very close and in front of them.
source: (I) Direction density of receiver animals, marginalized over distances, shows that female mice vocalize primarily when the male mouse's snout is very close and in front of them. Note that the overall angle of approach of the male mouse is not from directly ahead (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

source: Cam64 data was band-pass filtered with a frequency range adapted to the frequency content of each USV. Specifically, first the frequency range of the USV was estimated as the 10th–90th percentile of the set of most intense frequencies at each time point. Next, this range was broadened by 5 kHz at both ends, and then limited at the top end to 95 kHz. If this range exceeded 50 kHz, the lower end was set to 45 kHz.

evidence: This is a description of the beamforming method.
